definition:
Revelation is God making himself known. The Bible never pictures human beings climbing up to discover God by their own effort; it pictures God speaking first, uncovering what would otherwise stay hidden. Christians have traditionally described two kinds of revelation. General revelation is what God shows of himself to every person through the created world, the moral sense, and the ordinary goodness of life. Special revelation is what he makes known by particular acts and words in history: his dealings with Israel, the words of the prophets, the life, death, and resurrection of Jesus, and the teaching of the apostles. Scripture is the written form of that special revelation, the witness God gave so that what he said and did would not be lost. The church confesses that Scripture is breathed out by God and written by human authors in their own languages, styles, and settings, and that it carries God's own authority.

The biblical vocabulary is concrete. The Hebrew verb galah means ‘to uncover’ or ‘to lay bare’, and it is used when God reveals himself or his purposes (Deuteronomy 29:29, Amos 3:7). The Hebrew dabar means ‘word’, and often the thing or event a word announces, so that ‘the word of the LORD came’ to a prophet is an event, not only a sound. In Greek, apokalyptō and its noun apokalypsis mean ‘to unveil’ and ‘unveiling’; phaneroō means ‘to make visible’. The written word is graphē, ‘writing’ or ‘Scripture’, and the formula gegraptai, ‘it stands written’, appeals to it as settled. Paul's word for its origin in 2 Timothy 3:16 is theopneustos, ‘God-breathed’, a rare compound that says where Scripture comes from before it says anything about how it was produced.
ot:
The Bible opens with God speaking. In Genesis 1 the world comes into being by his word; each day begins with ‘And God said’ (Genesis 1:3), and creation itself becomes a kind of address. After the rebellion of Genesis 3 God still speaks first, calling to the hiding man, “Where are you?” (Genesis 3:9). Revelation in the Old Testament is never a human achievement; it is God taking the initiative with people who did not seek him. He calls Abram out of Ur (Genesis 12:1), appears to the patriarchs, and binds himself to them by promise. At the burning bush he tells Moses who he is and gives the covenant name, the LORD, as the name by which he is to be remembered in every generation (Exodus 3:14-15).

Sinai is the Old Testament's great scene of revelation. Moses reminds Israel that at Horeb “You heard the sound of the words, but saw no form; there was only a voice” (Deuteronomy 4:12). Israel's God is known by what he says and does, not by an image, which is why the second commandment forbids images. Sinai also begins Scripture as a written thing. “And Moses wrote down all the words of the LORD” (Exodus 24:4); the tablets of the covenant are written “by the finger of God” (Exodus 31:18); and the finished Book of the Law is placed beside the ark as a witness (Deuteronomy 31:24-26). Deuteronomy draws the line that governs the rest of the Bible: “The secret things belong to the LORD our God, but the things revealed belong to us and to our children forever” (Deuteronomy 29:29). God does not tell everything, but what he has told is given to be obeyed.

The prophets carried revelation into Israel's history. God promised a prophet like Moses and said, “I will put My words in his mouth” (Deuteronomy 18:18), and the same language returns when Jeremiah is called (Jeremiah 1:9). Amos says God does nothing “without revealing His plan to His servants the prophets” (Amos 3:7); the word behind ‘plan’ is sod, the confidential counsel of a council. Written prophecy could be destroyed and still not lost. When King Jehoiakim burned Jeremiah's scroll around 604 BC, Jeremiah dictated it again to Baruch, and more was added (Jeremiah 36:27-32). The written word also judged the people who kept it. During temple repairs in Josiah's reign, around 622 BC, the priest Hilkiah found the Book of the Law; when the king heard it read he tore his clothes and led a reform (2 Kings 22:8-13). After the exile Ezra read the Law aloud in Jerusalem while Levites explained it, “so that the people could understand what was being read” (Nehemiah 8:8), a scene that stands behind every later practice of reading and preaching Scripture in public.

The Psalms hold the two kinds of revelation side by side. Psalm 19 begins with the sky: “The heavens declare the glory of God; the skies proclaim the work of His hands” (Psalm 19:1). This speech is wordless, “Without speech or language” (Psalm 19:3), yet it reaches the whole earth. Then the psalm turns to the written word: “The Law of the LORD is perfect, reviving the soul” (Psalm 19:7). Creation tells of God's glory; the Law, torah in Hebrew, meaning ‘instruction’ more broadly than ‘legislation’, revives, makes wise, and gives joy. Psalm 119 spends 176 verses delighting in that word as a lamp and a light. Isaiah adds that God's word outlasts everything it addresses, “the word of our God stands forever” (Isaiah 40:8), and that it does what God sends it to do, like rain that waters the earth (Isaiah 55:10-11). The Old Testament also knows what it is to lose revelation. Samuel grew up when “the word of the LORD was rare and visions were scarce” (1 Samuel 3:1), and Amos threatens a famine “of hearing the words of the LORD” (Amos 8:11). To be left without God's word is itself a judgment.
nt:
The New Testament claims that all this speaking reached its goal in a person. “On many past occasions and in many different ways, God spoke to our fathers through the prophets. But in these last days He has spoken to us by His Son” (Hebrews 1:1-2). The Son is not one more messenger; he is “the radiance of God’s glory and the exact representation of His nature” (Hebrews 1:3). John opens his Gospel by calling him the Word, logos, who was with God and was God, and who “became flesh and made His dwelling among us” (John 1:14). John ends his prologue with the claim that sums up the New Testament doctrine of revelation: “No one has ever seen God, but the one and only Son, who is Himself God and is at the Father’s side, has made Him known” (John 1:18). The verb there, exēgeomai, was used for narrating or setting out in full; the Son is the one who tells God. Jesus says the same in his own words: no one knows the Father “except the Son and those to whom the Son chooses to reveal Him” (Matthew 11:27), and “Anyone who has seen Me has seen the Father” (John 14:9).

Jesus received the Hebrew Scriptures as the word of God. He said he came not to abolish the Law or the Prophets “but to fulfill them” (Matthew 5:17), rested an argument on a single word of a psalm with the remark that “the Scripture cannot be broken” (John 10:35), and told his opponents that the Scriptures they studied “testify about Me” (John 5:39). After the resurrection he opened the whole of Israel's Scripture to his disciples, “beginning with Moses and all the Prophets” (Luke 24:27), and named its three parts, “the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms” (Luke 24:44), which roughly correspond to the three divisions of the Hebrew Bible. He also promised that the Spirit would remind the apostles of what he had said and guide them “into all truth” (John 14:26, 16:13). The church has read those promises as the ground of the apostolic writings.

The apostles taught both kinds of revelation. Paul says that God's “eternal power and divine nature, have been clearly seen, being understood from His workmanship, so that men are without excuse” (Romans 1:20), and that the work of the law is written on the hearts of Gentiles who never had Moses (Romans 2:14-15). At Lystra he said God “has not left Himself without testimony to His goodness” in rain and harvest (Acts 14:17). Yet Paul also says that the saving purpose of God is a mystery concealed for ages and now revealed (Romans 16:25-26), and that what “No eye has seen, no ear has heard” God “has revealed it to us by the Spirit” (1 Corinthians 2:9-10). General revelation leaves every person accountable; special revelation tells the good news. The Thessalonians received Paul's preaching “not as the word of men, but as the true word of God” (1 Thessalonians 2:13), and Paul commands that his letters be read and his traditions held, whether spoken or written (2 Thessalonians 2:15).

Two passages became the church's classic texts on Scripture. Paul reminds Timothy that the Holy Scriptures he has known from infancy “are able to make you wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus” and that “All Scripture is God-breathed and is useful for instruction, for conviction, for correction, and for training in righteousness” (2 Timothy 3:15-16). The Scripture in view is first of all the Old Testament, and the purpose is practical: salvation and a life equipped for good works. Peter adds how it happened: “no such prophecy was ever brought forth by the will of man, but men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit” (2 Peter 1:21). The participle pheromenoi, ‘being carried’, comes from the same verb Luke uses in Acts 27:15 and 17 of a ship driven by the wind; the men still spoke, but the Spirit bore them. The same letter already places Paul's letters beside “the rest of the Scriptures” (2 Peter 3:16), which shows the apostolic writings being received as Scripture within the New Testament period itself. Luke describes his own careful research among eyewitnesses (Luke 1:1-4), a reminder that inspiration worked through human labor and not around it. The Bible closes with a warning against adding to or taking from “the words of this book of prophecy” (Revelation 22:18-19), which strictly concerns Revelation itself but has often been read as a fitting seal on the whole.

keyTexts.why: God's first act in Scripture is speech. Revelation begins with the God who speaks the world into being, so that creation itself carries his word.
At the burning bush God gives Moses his covenant name. Revelation is God disclosing who he is, not humans guessing.
At Sinai Israel heard words and saw no form. God is known through his word, which is why Israel may make no image of him.
The classic distinction between what God keeps hidden and what he has revealed for his people to know and obey.
The rediscovered Book of the Law judges king and people alike. The written word stands over the community that keeps it.
The heavens speak without words, and the Law revives the soul. The psalm holds general and special revelation together and gives each its task.
God's word is effective. Like rain it does not return empty, but accomplishes what he sends it to do.
Jesus came to fulfill, not abolish, the Law and the Prophets, and he affirms their lasting authority to the smallest stroke.
The risen Christ reads the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms as testimony to himself and opens his disciples' minds to understand them.
No one has seen God, but the Son has made him known. Christ is the fullness of revelation, the one in whom God is told.
God's power and divine nature are clearly seen in what he made, so that all are without excuse. The central text for general revelation.
The apostolic message was received as the word of God and not merely human words, and it is at work in those who believe.
All Scripture is God-breathed and able to make a person wise for salvation through faith in Christ. The foundation text for inspiration and the purpose of Scripture.
God spoke in many ways through the prophets and has now spoken by his Son, the exact representation of his nature.
Prophecy did not come by human will; men spoke from God as the Holy Spirit carried them. Human authorship and divine origin together.

history:
The early church inherited Israel's Scriptures and read them, with the apostles' writings, as the word of God. The pressure to say what counted as Scripture came from rivals. Around 144 Marcion, in Rome, rejected the Old Testament and accepted only an edited Luke and ten letters of Paul; around 180 Irenaeus of Lyon answered the gnostic teachers, who claimed secret traditions, by appealing to the public teaching handed down in the churches, to the rule of faith, and to four Gospels and no more. The Muratorian fragment, a list of accepted books traditionally dated to the late second century (some scholars argue for the fourth), shows the New Testament taking shape. In 367 Athanasius of Alexandria, in his thirty-ninth Festal Letter, listed exactly the twenty-seven books of the New Testament, and North African synods at Hippo (393) and Carthage (397) affirmed a list of the same books. Christians have generally described this as the church recognizing books that already carried authority rather than conferring it. The Old Testament canon was more complicated: Jerome preferred the books of the Hebrew Bible, while Augustine and the North African councils also received the books Protestants later called the Apocrypha and Catholics call deuterocanonical.

Medieval theology built on both kinds of revelation. Thomas Aquinas, in the Summa Theologiae begun around 1265, argued that some truths about God, such as his existence, can be known by natural reason, while others, such as the Trinity and the incarnation, are known only because God revealed them, and that even the first kind was also revealed for the sake of those who could not reason their way to it. The Reformation turned on authority. Martin Luther and the other Reformers held that Scripture is the final authority over the church's traditions, the principle later summarized as sola scriptura, and John Calvin taught in his Institutes (final edition 1559) that believers are persuaded of Scripture's authority by the inward testimony of the Holy Spirit, not by the church's decree. The Council of Trent, at its fourth session in 1546, answered that the gospel is contained in the written books and in unwritten apostolic traditions, both to be received with equal reverence, and defined the canon to include the deuterocanonical books.

The Protestant confessions set the doctrine in the form many churches still use. The Belgic Confession (1561) says God is known by two means, the creation, which it likens to a book, and his holy Word, which makes him known more fully. The Thirty-Nine Articles of the Church of England (1563) affirm that Scripture contains all things necessary to salvation. The Westminster Confession (1646) opens with Scripture: the light of nature leaves people without excuse but cannot give the saving knowledge of God, so he committed his revelation to writing; the sixty-six books are the Word of God; their authority rests on God, not on the church; and the things necessary for salvation are clear enough that the unlearned can grasp them by ordinary means. Eastern Orthodox churches, for their part, have held Scripture as the heart of Holy Tradition rather than a rival to it.

Modern debates reopened the question from several sides. Historical criticism, from the eighteenth century on, examined the Bible as ancient literature and often denied that it was revealed at all. In response B. B. Warfield, who taught at Princeton Seminary from 1887 to 1921, set out the doctrine of plenary verbal inspiration. Karl Barth, in the first volume of his Church Dogmatics (1932), described the Word of God in three forms: revealed in Christ, written in Scripture, and proclaimed in preaching. The First Vatican Council (1870) taught that God can be known with certainty from created things by the natural light of reason, and the Second Vatican Council's constitution Dei Verbum (1965) described revelation as God's self-communication and taught that Scripture teaches without error the truth God wanted recorded for the sake of salvation. Among evangelicals the Lausanne Covenant (1974) affirmed Scripture as without error in all that it affirms, and the Chicago Statement on Biblical Inerrancy (1978) set out inerrancy in a series of affirmations and denials. The site's full treatment at /theology/doctrine/scripture surveys these views at length.

differ.body: Because God cannot lie and Scripture is breathed out by God, the Bible is without error in everything it affirms, including what it says about history and the natural world. This view does not demand wooden literalism: it allows for round numbers, ordinary descriptive speech such as sunrise, loose quotation, and the conventions of ancient writing, and it applies inerrancy to the original manuscripts. Its defenders, from B. B. Warfield to the framers of the 1978 Chicago Statement, argue that Jesus treated Scripture as unbreakable down to single words, and that a Bible which errs where it can be checked gives no secure ground for trusting it where it cannot.

Scripture never fails in what God gave it to do: to make people wise for salvation and to teach faith and life. Its descriptions of nature and some details of history speak in the ordinary language and assumptions of the people God used, and that is not a defect but the shape of God's condescension, his stooping to human speech. Defenders such as G. C. Berkouwer and Donald Bloesch argue that 2 Timothy 3:15-17 itself names the Bible's purpose, and that requiring modern technical precision asks the Bible to be a kind of book it never claimed to be. They hold its authority as fully as anyone and locate its truthfulness in what it intends to teach.

Roman Catholic and Eastern Orthodox Christians, and many Protestants who take the ancient church seriously, hold that Scripture is inspired and authoritative and that it is rightly received and read within the church that recognized the canon and handed it on. For Catholics, Scripture and apostolic Tradition flow from the same divine source, and the church's teaching office serves the word by interpreting it; for the Orthodox, Scripture is the heart of Holy Tradition. They point to 2 Thessalonians 2:15, where Paul commends both spoken and written traditions, and argue that no one reads the Bible from nowhere; the church's long memory protects the reader from making the text say what the moment wants.

differ.view: Scripture as witness to the Word
differ.body: Karl Barth and theologians influenced by him hold that revelation in the strict sense is God's own act of speaking, whose center is Jesus Christ. Scripture is the human witness to that revelation, chosen and used by God, so that through it God speaks his Word again and again. Barth taught that the prophets and apostles were fallible human beings whose words God nevertheless takes up, and he refused to make any theory of the text the ground of faith. Defenders argue that this keeps the living God, not a doctrine about a book, at the center, and that it takes seriously Hebrews 1:1-2, where God's final word is a person.

errors:
The church has rejected several distortions. Marcion's rejection of the Old Testament, which set the God of Israel against the Father of Jesus, was refused because Jesus and the apostles received Israel's Scriptures as the word of their own God; a Bible without the Old Testament has cut its gospel off at the root. The gnostic claim to secret revelation given only to insiders was refused because Christian revelation is public, handed on openly in the churches and written down. Later groups that claimed new revelation equal to or above Scripture, or prophets whose words could correct the apostles, have been rejected for the same reason: the apostolic witness is the foundation (Ephesians 2:20), and later claims are tested by it.

Two opposite errors about how Scripture was produced have also been rejected by most of the church. One treats the Bible as a merely human book, a record of Israel's and the church's religious experience and nothing more, which cannot account for the Bible's own claim that God spoke through it. The other treats it as dictated in a way that erases its authors, as if Luke's research, Paul's temper, and the psalmists' tears were not really theirs; 2 Peter 1:21 insists that men spoke, even as the Spirit carried them. A third error confuses respect for Scripture with ignoring what kind of writing it is, reading poetry as chemistry or parable as chronicle, which honors the words while missing what God is saying through them.
life:
If God has spoken, the first posture of a Christian is listening. That changes how a person reads the Bible: not as a manual to be consulted when convenient or a quarry for proof texts, but as the place where the living God addresses them. It also changes how a person looks at the world. The sky, the harvest, and the conscience are not mute; they tell of a Maker, even when people refuse to hear. Christians who hold this doctrine read the Bible slowly, in context, with others, and expect to be corrected by it rather than to use it to correct everyone else.

It also shapes prayer and hope. Prayer becomes an answer to a God who spoke first, which is why so many Christian prayers are drawn from the Psalms and the words of Scripture. And because God's word stands forever while grass withers, a person who has built on it has somewhere to stand when opinions, institutions, and their own feelings shift. The doctrine does not promise that every hard passage will be easy; Peter himself said some of Paul's letters are hard to understand. It promises that the God who speaks does not lie, and that he has said enough for a person to know him, trust him, and live.
questions: Psalm 19 moves from the wordless speech of the heavens to the Law that revives the soul. What can creation tell a person about God, and what can it not tell?
Hebrews 1:1-2 says God has spoken finally in his Son. How should that shape the way a Christian reads the Old Testament and the rest of the New?
2 Peter 1:21 says men spoke as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit. What difference does it make that Scripture is both fully human and from God?
